# Bicriteria Approximate Navigable Graphs in General Metrics

Hongyi Chen<sup>∗</sup><tbc>

<tbc>Tianyi Zhang<sup>†</sup><tbc>

**Abstract**

We study approximation algorithms for constructing sparse navigable graphs in general metrics. Given an _n_-point metric (_P_,d) and a parameter \(\alpha\ge 1\), an \(\alpha\)-navigable graph is a directed graph _G_=(_P,E_) such that for every ordered pair of distinct points \(s,t\in P\), the vertex _s_ has an outgoing edge (_s,p_) with d(_p,t_) < d(_s,t_) / \(\alpha\). The objective is to minimize the number of edges. The study of approximation algorithms for sparse navigable graphs in general metrics was recently initiated by Khanna, Padaki, and Waingarten (SODA 2026), and independently by Conway et al. (SODA 2026). These works show that the single-criterion problem faces a Set Cover barrier: an _O_(log_n_)-approximation is achievable, whereas obtaining an _o_(log_n_)-approximation is NP-hard. To obtain faster algorithms, Khanna, Padaki, and Waingarten (SODA 2026) introduced bicriteria approximation, in which the output graph is required to be \(\alpha\)-navigable, while its size is compared against that of an optimal \(\beta\)-navigable graph for some relaxed parameter \(\beta\ge\alpha\). They gave a fast matrix-multiplication-based algorithm that computes an \((\alpha,2(1+\varepsilon)\alpha)\)-bicriteria _O_(log_n_)-approximation in time \(\widetilde{O}(n\omega log\Delta/\varepsilon)\), where \(\Delta\) denotes the aspect ratio and \(\omega\) is the matrix multiplication exponent. Our main result is a simpler near-quadratic-time algorithm with stronger bicriteria guarantees. For every constant \(\alpha\ge 1\), we compute in time \(\widetilde{O}(n2log\Delta)\) an \(\alpha\)-navigable graph that is simultaneously an \((\alpha,2\alpha+O(1))\)-bicriteria _O_(1)-approximation and an \((\alpha,\alpha+O(1))\)-bicriteria _O_(log_n_)-approximation. We complement the algorithm with a hardness result showing that for every constant \(\eta\in(0,1)\), no polynomial-time algorithm can compute an \((\alpha,2\alpha-\eta)\)-bicriteria _o_(log_n_)-approximation unless P = NP.

<sup>∗</sup>State Key Laboratory for Novel Software Technology, Nanjing University, `hychener01@gmail.com` <sup>†</sup>State Key Laboratory for Novel Software Technology, Nanjing University, `tianyiz25@nju.edu.cn`

## 1 Introduction.

Nearest neighbor search has been a fundamental problem in computer science \[Ben75, KOR98, IM98, JDS10, MY16\], with wide applications in modern AI systems \[JDJ19, LPP<sup>+</sup>20, GXG<sup>+</sup>23\]. In this problem, we are given a point set _P_ together with a pairwise distance function \(\mathsf{d}(\cdot,\cdot)\), and the goal is to build an efficient data structure which (approximately) answers \(argmin_{p\in P}\mathsf{d}(p,q)\) for a query point _q_ in the underlying metric space. Locality-sensitive hashing has been a classical approach with abundant theoretical studies for this problem \[AIL<sup>+</sup>15\], but it becomes inefficient for large high-dimensional datasets. A recent line of practical work has adopted graph-based paradigms, including HNSW \[MY16\], NSG \[FXWC17\], and DiskANN \[SDK<sup>+</sup>19\]; these heuristic approaches have yielded impressive empirical performance on real-world datasets \[WXYW21, AEP25\]. A central theoretical abstraction behind graph-based search is _navigability_, which is defined as follows.

**Definition 1.1** (\[SDK<sup>+</sup>19, IX23\])**.** Given a constant parameter \(\alpha\ge 1\), for any ordered pair \((s,t)\in P\times P\) with \(s\neq t\) and any point \(u\in P\), we say that a directed edge (_s,u_) is an \(\alpha\)_-navigation from s to t_ if

\(\mathsf{d}(u,t)<\frac{\mathsf{d}(s,t)}{\alpha}.\)

A directed graph _G_=(_P,E_) is said to be \(\alpha\)_-navigable_ if for every ordered pair \((s,t)\in P\times P\) with \(s\neq t\), the vertex _s_ has at least one outgoing edge that forms an \(\alpha\)-navigation toward _t_.

Graph-based nearest-neighbor search methods typically proceed in two stages. In the preprocessing stage, one builds a navigable graph _G_=(_P,E_) on the dataset. At query time, many such methods perform a greedy or greedy-search-like traversal over _G_: starting from one or several entry points, they repeatedly inspect out-neighbors of currently active vertices and try to move the search toward points closer to the query. Thus, the quality of the graph is governed by two competing requirements: the graph should contain enough edges to satisfy the navigation constraints, but it should also be sparse so that memory usage and the cost of inspecting neighbors remain small. It was shown in \[IX23\] that, for any \(\alpha>1\), any \(\alpha\)-navigable graph can be used to construct a data structure which returns \(\left(\frac{\alpha+1}{\alpha-1}+\epsilon\right)\)-approximate nearest neighbors in \(O\left(log_\alpha\frac{\Delta}{(\alpha-1)\epsilon}\right)\) greedy steps, where \(\Delta\) is the aspect ratio of the metric, namely the ratio of the maximum to the minimum distance between distinct points of _P_.

This motivates the following problem: given an _n_-point metric space (_P,_d) and a parameter \(\alpha\ge 1\), construct an \(\alpha\)-navigable graph using as few edges as possible. The authors of \[DGM<sup>+</sup>24\] showed that every set of _n_ distinct points admits a 1-navigable graph with \(\widetilde{O}(n^{3/2})^1\) edges, and gave a \(\widetilde{O}(n^2)\)-time construction. In a different direction, Arya and Mount \[AM93\] showed that, for point sets in _d_-dimensional Euclidean space, one can construct a 1-navigable graph with maximum degree 2<sup>_O(d_)</sup>. However, they are not instance-optimal: a particular input _P_ may admit a much sparser navigable graph than the worst-case bound.

Two recent concurrent works \[KPW26, CDFC<sup>+</sup>26\] have initiated the study of approximation algorithms for constructing sparse \(\alpha\)-navigable graphs in general metrics. In both works, the authors showed a reduction from Set Cover to \(\alpha\)-navigable graphs, establishing NP-hardness of _o_(log_n_)- approximations of the sparsest \(\alpha\)-navigable graphs. On the algorithmic side, both works designed an \(\tilde{O}\left(min\{n\cdot OPT_\alpha,n^{2.5}\}\right)\) time algorithm which computes _O_(log_n_)-approximations of the sparsest \(\alpha\)-navigable graphs, where \(OPT_\alpha\) is the number of edges in the optimal solution. Besides, for the special case of \(\alpha=1\), the authors of \[CDFC<sup>+</sup>26\] showed a \(\tilde{O}(n^2)\) time algorithm with _O_(log_n_)- approximation. For general values of \(\alpha\ge 1\), to achieve faster runtime, the authors of \[KPW26\] have studied the notion of bicriteria approximation of \(\alpha\)-navigable graphs defined below.

<sup>1</sup>\(\tilde{O}\) hides poly-logarithmic factors.

**Definition 1.2** (\[KPW26\])**.** Let (_P,_d) be a finite metric space and \(\beta\ge\alpha\ge 1\). A directed graph _G_=(_P,E_) is a \((\alpha,\beta)\)_-bricriteria c-approximation_ to the sparsest \(\alpha\)-navigable graph if _G_ is \(\alpha\)-navigable and

\(|E|\le c\cdot min_H\text{is}\beta\text{-navigable}|E(H)|.\)

To unify notation, the single criterion problem of approximating \(\alpha\)-navigable graphs can be written as a \((\alpha,\alpha)\)-bricriteria problem. In \[KPW26\], it was shown that a \((\alpha,2(1+\epsilon)\alpha)\)-bricriteria _O_(log_n_)-approximation can be computed by an algorithm in \(\tilde{O}(n^\omega log\Delta/\epsilon)\) time, where \(\Delta\) is the aspect ratio of metric (_P,_d) and \(\omega\) is the matrix multiplication exponent. The following question was left open in \[KPW26\].

_Question_ 1.3. Is there a quadratic-time algorithm for (bricriteria) _O_(log_n_)-approximation of the sparsest \(\alpha\)-navigable graph?

## 1.1 Our Results.

As our main algorithmic result, we answer Question 1.3 affirmatively up to polylogarithmic factors in the bicriteria setting. More precisely, we give a near-quadratic-time construction whose bicriteria guarantees improve upon the previous fastest algorithm and are essentially tight in the large-\(\alpha\) regime.

**Theorem 1.4.** _Let_ (_P,_d) _be an n-point metric space with aspect ratio_ \(\Delta\) _and_ \(\alpha\ge 1\) _be a constant parameter. Then, there is an algorithm with runtime_ \(\tilde{O}(n^2log\Delta)\) _which builds an_ \(\alpha\)_-navigable graph G_=(_P,E_) _with the following bicriteria approximation guarantees simultaneously._

• _G is an_ \((\alpha,\beta)\)_-bricriteria_ 5_-approximation, where_ \(\beta=2\alpha+8+4/\alpha\le 2\alpha+12\);<tbc>

• _G is an_ \((\alpha,\beta')\)_-bricriteria O_(ln_n)-approximation, where_ \(\beta'=\alpha+5+2/\alpha\le\alpha+7\).

The first guarantee shows that the Set Cover barrier can be bypassed by allowing an almost factor-2 relaxation in the bicriteria parameter: instead of an _O_(log_n_)-approximation, we obtain a constant-factor approximation against the sparsest \((2\alpha+O(1))\)-navigable graph. The second guarantee gives an _O_(log_n_)-approximation with a smaller bicriteria loss than the previous fast bicriteria algorithm of \[KPW26\]; in particular, for large constant \(\alpha\), the leading coefficient improves from roughly \(2\alpha\) to roughly \(\alpha\). Another main contribution is the running time: both guarantees are achieved in \(\widetilde{O}(n^2log\Delta)\) time, improving over the \(\widetilde{O}(n^\omega log\Delta/\epsilon)\)-time fast bicriteria algorithm of \[KPW26\]. Since the input metric is specified by \(\Theta(n^2)\) pairwise distances, this running time is optimal up to logarithmic factors if pairwise distances are given explicitly.

Our second result shows that the factor 2 appearing above is essentially unavoidable. Below \(2\alpha\), the Set Cover barrier persists.

**Theorem 1.5.** _For every constant_ \(\alpha\ge 1\) _and every constant_ \(\eta\in(0,1)\)_, there exists a constant_ \(c_\eta>0\) _such that it is NP-hard to compute an_ \((\alpha,2\alpha-\eta)\)_-bricriteria_ \(c_\eta lnn\)_-approximation of the sparsest_ \(\alpha\)_-navigable graph on a metric_ (_P,_d) _with n points._

Together with Theorem 1.4, Theorem 1.5 shows that our two upper-bound guarantees are nearly optimal in complementary ways. First, the lower bound shows that the Set Cover barrier persists for every bicriteria parameter strictly below \(2\alpha\): even if the algorithm is allowed to compare against the sparsest \((2\alpha-\eta)\)-navigable graph, an _o_(log_n_)-approximation remains NP-hard. Therefore, in the entire sub-\(2\alpha\) bicriteria regime, the best possible approximation factor is \(\Theta(logn)\); our \((\alpha,\alpha+O(1))\)-bricriteria _O_(log_n_)-approximation matches this approximation factor while using bicriteria<tbc>

<tbc>loss \(\alpha+O(1)=(1+o_\alpha(1))\alpha\), which is asymptotically the smallest possible since every bicriteria comparison must have \(\beta\ge\alpha\). Second, the same lower bound shows that any constant-factor approximation must cross the \(2\alpha\) threshold, while our \((\alpha,2\alpha+O(1))\)-bicriteria _O_(1)-approximation does so by only an additive constant. Thus, for large \(\alpha\), our results identify \(2\alpha\) as the sharp threshold for beating the logarithmic Set Cover barrier, and achieve essentially the smallest bicriteria loss possible on the logarithmic-approximation side of this threshold.

We emphasize that our main focus is the regime where \(\alpha\) is large. This is precisely the regime in which the standard theoretical guarantee for greedy search becomes meaningful for high-accuracy nearest-neighbor search: on an \(\alpha\)-navigable graph, greedy search achieves approximation ratio \(\frac{\alpha+1}{\alpha-1}+\varepsilon\). Since \(\frac{\alpha+1}{\alpha-1}=1+\frac{2}{\alpha-1}\), obtaining a \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximate nearest neighbor through this analysis requires \(\alpha=\Theta(1/\varepsilon)\), after choosing the additive accuracy parameter \(\varepsilon\) appropriately. In this sense, our construction gives a nearly tight bicriteria approximation in the theoretically relevant high-accuracy regime.

We note that in practice, the values of \(\alpha\) used or observed in proximity graphs are often smaller than 2 \[SDK<sup>+</sup>19\]. However, the nearest neighbor approximation guarantee of greedy search on \(\alpha\)-navigable graphs for small choices of \(\alpha\) is still poorly understood, and this is beyond the scope of the present work.

## 1.2 Technical Overview.

We give an overview of the main ideas behind our upper bound. We start with the Set Cover viewpoint, which explains the _O_(log_n_) barrier in previous work. We then describe a simple but slower ordered-greedy procedure, which exposes the packing principle behind the \(2\alpha\) threshold. Our algorithm can be viewed as an acceleration of the ordered-greedy procedure, achieved by replacing the source-specific greedy choices with globally shared representatives.

### The Set Cover viewpoint.

For a fixed source point _s_, the \(\alpha\)-navigability constraints can be written as a Set Cover instance. The universe is _P_\\{_s_}, and each candidate out-neighbor \(u\neq s\) corresponds to the set

\(Z_\alpha(s,u)=\left\{t\in P\backslash\{s\}\middle|\mathsf{d}(u,t)<\frac{\mathsf{d}(s,t)}{\alpha}\right\}.\)

Choosing out-neighborhoods for _s_ is therefore exactly the problem of covering all targets \(t\in P\backslash\{s\}\) by sets \(Z_\alpha(s,u)\). Constructing a sparsest \(\alpha\)-navigable graph amounts to solving one such Set Cover instance for every source _s_.

This formulation immediately yields _O_(log_n_)-approximation algorithms via greedy Set Cover, and it also explains why the problem inherits the classical Set Cover hardness barrier. Previous algorithms [KPW26, CDFC<sup>+</sup>26] for sparse navigable graphs in general metrics are based on this viewpoint. However, if one wants to beat the _O_(log_n_) approximation factor, the Set Cover formulation by itself does not reveal enough additional structure.

## Warm-up: source-wise ordered greedy.

Fix a source _s_ and consider the following simple greedy procedure. Process all targets \(t\in P\backslash\{s\}\) in nondecreasing order of d(_s,t_). Whenever no previously added outgoing edge of _s_ is an \(\alpha\)-navigation from _s_ to the current target _t_, add the edge (_s,t_). This procedure clearly produces an \(\alpha\)-navigable graph, since any uncovered target can always be covered by selecting itself. Let _p_<sub>1</sub>_,p_<sub>2</sub>_,...,p<sub>k</sub>_ be the out-neighbors selected for source _s_, in nondecreasing order of their distance from _s_. When _p<sub>j</sub>_ is selected, none of the previously added edges (_s,p<sub>i</sub>),i\<j_, is an \(\alpha\)-navigation from _s_ to _p<sub>j</sub>_. Therefore,

\(\mathsf{d}(p_i,p_j)\ge\frac{\mathsf{d}(s,p_j)}{\alpha}\text{for every}i<j.\) (1.1)

Now compare this ordered-greedy solution with any \(2\alpha\)-navigable graph _H_. For every selected point _p<sub>j</sub>_, the graph _H_ contains an out-neighbor _u<sub>j</sub>_ of _s_ such that<tbc>

\(\mathsf{d}(u_j,p_j)<\frac{\mathsf{d}(s,p_j)}{2\alpha}.\)

<tbc>Choose one such out-neighbor _u<sub>j</sub>_ for each selected point _p<sub>j</sub>_. We show that the map \(p_j\mapsto u_j\) is injective, which bounds the number of selected points by the out-degree of _s_ in _H_. Indeed, suppose two selected points _p<sub>i</sub>,p<sub>j</sub>_ with _i\<j_ were mapped to the same out-neighbor _u_. Then by triangle inequality,

\(\mathsf{d}(p_i,p_j)\le\mathsf{d}(p_i,u)+\mathsf{d}(u,p_j)<\frac{\mathsf{d}(s,p_i)}{2\alpha}+\frac{\mathsf{d}(s,p_j)}{2\alpha}\le\frac{\mathsf{d}(s,p_j)}{\alpha},\)

where the last inequality uses \(\mathsf{d}(s,p_i)\le\mathsf{d}(s,p_j)\). This contradicts (1.1). Hence, for this fixed source _s_, the ordered-greedy procedure selects no more out-neighbors than the out-degree of _s_ in any \(2\alpha\)-navigable graph.

However, this ordered-greedy procedure is too slow for our purposes. Running it independently for all sources requires repeatedly testing whether each target is already navigated by one of the previously selected out-neighbors. A direct implementation takes _O(n_<sup>3</sup>) time in the worst case.

## Global acceleration via hierarchical covers.

Our starting point is the classical use of nets and hierarchical covers, which has been widely adopted in low-dimensional Euclidean and doubling metrics [KL04, LT25]. Instead of running greedy independently for every source, we precompute globally shared representatives at multiple distance scales. More concretely, let \(r_i=\left(1+\frac{1}{\alpha}\right)^i\) range over the relevant distance scales. At each scale _r<sub>i</sub>_, we use balls of radius \(\Theta(r_i/\alpha)\) and, for each source _s_, add edges to selected centers lying in an appropriate annulus around _s_. The annulus is chosen so that if a target _t_ satisfies d(_s,t_)≈_r<sub>i</sub>_, and _p_ is the center covering _t_ at scale _i_, then _p_ is included as an out-neighbor of _s_ and

\(\mathsf{d}(p,t)<\frac{\mathsf{d}(s,t)}{\alpha}.\)

Hence (_s,p_) is an \(\alpha\)-navigation from _s_ to _t_, and taking all sources and scales gives an \(\alpha\)-navigable graph.

The two approximation guarantees use two closely related but different choices of global representatives. For the constant-factor guarantee, we use separated covers: at each scale, the selected centers are pairwise farther than the ball radius. This separation is a coarse, scale-by-scale analogue of the ordered-greedy packing condition above. For each fixed source _s_, this separation allows us to map the selected centers at each scale to outgoing edges of _s_ in a sparsest \((2\alpha+O(1))\)-navigable graph. The map is injective at each scale, and each edge is used by these maps at only constantly many scales.

For the logarithmic guarantee, we instead use the standard greedy Set Cover algorithm over all radius-\(\Theta(r_i/\alpha)\) balls, allowing the chosen center to be a point that has already been covered. This variant does not have the separation property used in the constant-factor analysis. For each source and scale, the clusters whose centers lie in the annulus define a local set-cover instance. We show that the number of selected centers is at most _O_(log_n_) times the optimum of this local instance. We then bound each local optimum by the number of outgoing edges of the source in a sparsest \((\alpha+O(1))\)-navigable graph that navigate to points in the local instance. Each such edge is counted at only constantly many scales.

Finally, to obtain the simultaneous statement of Theorem 1.4, we run both constructions and return the graph with fewer edges. Since both candidate graphs are \(\alpha\)-navigable, the returned graph is \(\alpha\)-navigable; because its size is no larger than either candidate, it inherits both bicriteria bounds.

## 2 Bicriteria Approximation in Near-Quadratic Time.

### 2.1 Algorithm Description.

Let (_P,_d) be a finite metric space on _n_ points and let \(\alpha\ge 1\) be a fixed parameter. By rescaling all distances by a common positive factor, we assume that the minimum nonzero pairwise distance is \(1+1/\alpha\). Consequently, all nonzero pairwise distances lie in the range \(\left[1+\frac{1}{\alpha}\right]\), \(\left(1+\frac{1}{\alpha}\right)\Delta\right]\), where \(\Delta\) is the aspect ratio of the metric. For any \(s\in P\) and radius parameter _r\>_0, define<tbc>

\(B(s,r)=\{u\in P|\mathsf{d}(s,u)\le r\}.\)

<tbc>Let \(\delta=1/\alpha\), let \(L=\left\lceil\mathrm{log}_{1+\delta}\Delta\right\rceil\), and define \(r_i=(1+\delta)^i\) for every \(0\le i\le L+1\). Notice that _r_<sub>0</sub>=1 and \(r_{L+1}\ge(1+\delta)\Delta\). Hence, for every pair of distinct points \(s,t\in P\), there exists an index \(0\le i\le L\) such that \(r_i<\mathsf{d}(s,t)\le r_{i+1}\). We use the following annulus around a source point _s_ at level _i_:

\(A_i(s)=\left\{v\in P:r_i-\frac{r_i}{\alpha+2}<\mathsf{d}(s,v)\le r_{i+1}+\frac{r_i}{\alpha+2}\right\}.\)

We use two different ball-cover routines. The first one is a separated cover and is used for the constant-factor bicriteria approximation. The second one is the usual greedy Set Cover algorithm over metric balls and is used for the logarithmic bicriteria approximation.

#### Separated ball cover.

Given a radius _r\>_0, the following procedure partitions _P_ into clusters _C_ with centers _p_ satisfying \(C\subseteq B(p,r)\). The centers are pairwise separated by distance strictly larger than _r_.

For every pair (_C,p_) returned by Algorithm 2.1, we have \(C\subseteq B(p,r)\). Moreover, if _p_ is chosen before another center \(p'\), then \(p'\) is not covered by _B(p,r_), and hence \(\mathsf{d}(p,p')>r\). Thus all centers are pairwise separated by distance more than _r_.

Output: a collection N of pairs (C,p), where the sets C partition P and \(C\subseteq B(p,r)\)
\(\mathcal{N}\leftarrow\emptyset\), \(U\leftarrow P\)
while \(U\neq\emptyset\) do
Choose an arbitrary point \(p\in U\)
\(C\leftarrow U\cap B(p,r)\), \(U\leftarrow U\backslash C\)
Add (C,p) to N
return N ### Greedy ball cover. For the logarithmic approximation, we instead run the standard greedy Set Cover algorithm where the universe is P and the available sets are all radius-r balls centered at points of P. Importantly, the center chosen at a step is allowed to be a point that has already been covered. Input: metric (P,d), radius r\>0
Output: a collection G of pairs (C,p), where the sets C partition P and \(C\subseteq B(p,r)\)
\(\mathcal{G}\leftarrow\emptyset\), \(U\leftarrow P\)
while \(U\neq\emptyset\) do
Choose \(p\in P\) maximizing \(|U\cap B(p,r)|\)
\(C\leftarrow U\cap B(p,r)\), \(U\leftarrow U\backslash C\)

Unlike Algorithm 2.1, the center p need not belong to the currently uncovered set U and need not belong to the cluster C. ### The constant-approximation construction. At every level i, we compute a separated ball cover with radius \(r_i/(\alpha+2)\). For each source s, we add edges to the centers that lie in the annulus Ai(s). ### The logarithmic-approximation construction. The logarithmic construction is identical except that the level covers are produced by the greedy Set Cover routine. ## 2.2 Running Time. Both ball-cover routines can be implemented in \(\tilde{O}(n^2)\) time for a fixed radius. First compute all radius-r balls. During the covering process, maintain the number of uncovered points in each ball. Whenever a cluster C is removed from the uncovered set, update the counters of all balls containing each point of C; this costs \(\tilde{O}(n|C|)\) time for the iteration and \(\tilde{O}(n^2)\) time over all iterations. A priority queue with lazy updates gives the required maximum-coverage choice in Algorithm 2.2. There are \(L+1=O(\alpha log\Delta)\) levels. For either graph construction, computing all covers therefore takes \(\tilde{O}(\alpha n^2log\Delta)\) time. Once the covers are computed, all edge sets can be constructed by checking, for every level i, every source s, and every selected center p, whether \(p\in A_i(s)\). Thus both Algorithm 2.3 and Algorithm 2.4 run in \(\tilde{O}(\alpha n^2\mathrm{log}\Delta)\) time, which is \(\tilde{O}(n^2\mathrm{log}\Delta)\) for constant \(\alpha\). ## 2.3 Proof of Correctness. **Lemma 2.1** (Ball Coverage)**.** _Let_ (P,d) _be a metric space and let_ \(\alpha\ge 1\)_. For any_ \(u,c,v\in P\)_, if_ \(\mathsf{d}(c,v)<\frac{\mathsf{d}(c,u)}{\alpha+1},\) _then the directed edge_ (u,c) _is an_ \(\alpha\)_-navigation from u to v, i.e.,_ \(\mathsf{d}(c,v)<\frac{\mathsf{d}(u,v)}{\alpha}.\) **Algorithm 2.3:** ConstantApproxNavigable\(\mathrm{Graph}(P,\mathsf{d},\alpha)\) **Algorithm 2.4:** LogApproxNavigable\(\mathrm{Graph}(P,\mathsf{d},\alpha)\)

<tbc>_Proof._ By triangle inequality,<tbc>

\(\mathsf{d}(u,v)\ge\mathsf{d}(c,u)-\mathsf{d}(c,v).\)

<tbc>Thus it suffices to prove

\(\mathsf{d}(c,v)<\frac{\mathsf{d}(c,u)-\mathsf{d}(c,v)}{\alpha},\)

which is equivalent to \((\alpha+1)\mathsf{d}(c,v)<\mathsf{d}(c,u)\). This is exactly the assumption.

**Lemma 2.2.** _Both algorithms_ (_Algorithms 2.3 and 2.4_) _compute_ \(\alpha\)_-navigable graphs for_ (_P,_d).

_Proof._ The proof only uses the following common property of the level-_i_ cover: its clusters form a partition of _P_, and each cluster _C_ with center _p_ satisfies \(C\subseteq B(p,r_i/(\alpha+2))\).

Fix one of the two algorithms, a source point \(s\in P\), and a target point \(t\in P\) with \(s\neq t\). Let _i_ be an index such that \(r_i<\mathsf{d}(s,t)\le r_{i+1}\); such an index exists by the scaling assumption. Since the level-_i_ clusters cover _P_, the point _t_ lies in some cluster _C_ with center _p_, and hence<tbc>

\(\mathsf{d}(t,p)\le\frac{r_i}{\alpha+2}.\)

<tbc>By triangle inequality,<tbc>

\(\mathsf{d}(s,p)\le\mathsf{d}(s,t)+\mathsf{d}(t,p)\le r_{i+1}+\frac{r_i}{\alpha+2},\)

<tbc>and

\(\mathsf{d}(s,p)\ge\mathsf{d}(s,t)-\mathsf{d}(t,p)>r_i-\frac{r_i}{\alpha+2}.\)

Thus \(p\in A_i(s)\), so the algorithm adds the edge (_s,p_).

Finally,

\(\frac{\mathsf{d}(p,s)}{\alpha+1}>\frac{1}{\alpha+1}\left(r_i-\frac{r_i}{\alpha+2}\right)=\frac{r_i}{\alpha+2}\ge\mathsf{d}(p,t).\)

Thus \(\mathsf{d}(p,t)<\mathsf{d}(p,s)/(\alpha+1)\). By Lemma 2.1, the edge (_s,p_) is an \(\alpha\)-navigation from _s_ to _t_. Since this holds for every distinct pair \(s,t\in P\), the output graph is \(\alpha\)-navigable.

## 2.4 Constant Bicriteria Approximation.

**Lemma 2.3.** _Let_ (_P,_d) _be a metric space of n points and let_ \(\alpha\ge 1\)_. Let G_=(_P,E_) _be the graph returned by Algorithm 2.3. Then G is an_ \((\alpha,\beta)\)_-bicriteria_ 5_-approximation, where_

\(\beta=2(1+\delta)(\alpha+2)+2=2\alpha+8+\frac{4}{\alpha}.\)

_Proof._ Let _G<sup>⋆</sup>_=(_P,E<sup>⋆</sup>_) be a sparsest \(\beta\)-navigable graph, and fix a source vertex \(s\in P\). Write \(E_s^\star=\{(s,x)\in E^\star\}\) for the out-edges of _s_ in _G<sup>⋆</sup>_.

Since \(E_s=\bigcup_{i=0}^LE_s^i\), we have \(|E_s|\le\sum_{i=0}^L|E_s^i|\). To bound this sum, we consider all pairs (_i,p_) such that \((s,p)\in E_s^i\); the same center _p_ is counted separately at different levels. For each such pair, the \(\beta\)-navigability of _G<sup>⋆</sup>_ guarantees an edge \((s,x)\in E_s^\star\) such that

\(\mathsf{d}(x,p)<\frac{\mathsf{d}(s,p)}{\beta}.\)

Choose one such edge and define \(\phi_s(i,p)=(s,x)\).

**Claim 2.4.** _For each fixed level i, the map_ \(p\mapsto\phi_s(i,p)\) _is injective on_ \(\{p\in P|(s,p)\in E_s^i\}\).

_Proof of claim._ Suppose that two distinct centers \(p,p'\in A_i(s)\) at level _i_ are both mapped to the same edge \((s,x)\in E_s^\star\). By triangle inequality, \(\mathsf{d}(p,p')\le\mathsf{d}(p,x)+\mathsf{d}(x,p')<\frac{\mathsf{d}(s,p)}{\beta}+\frac{\mathsf{d}(s,p')}{\beta}.\) Since \(p,p'\in A_i(s)\), \(\mathsf{d}(s,p),\mathsf{d}(s,p')\le r_{i+1}+\frac{r_i}{\alpha+2},\) and therefore \(\mathsf{d}(p,p')<\frac{2\left((1+\delta)+\frac{1}{\alpha+2}\right)r_i}{\beta}.\) On the other hand, the centers returned by Algorithm 2.1 at level _i_ are separated by distance more than \(r_i/(\alpha+2)\). Hence \(\frac{r_i}{\alpha+2}<\mathsf{d}(p,p')<\frac{2\left((1+\delta)+\frac{1}{\alpha+2}\right)r_i}{\beta},\) which implies \(\beta<2(1+\delta)(\alpha+2)+2.\) This contradicts the definition of \(\beta\). **Claim 2.5.** _For every edge_ \((s,x)\in E_s^\star\)_, there are at most_ 5 _indices i for which some p with_ \((s,p)\in E_s^i\) _satisfies_ \(\phi_s(i,p)=(s,x)\). _Proof of claim._ Suppose that \(p\in A_i(s)\) is a level-_i_ center and \(\phi_s(i,p)=(s,x)\). By definition of \(\phi_s\), \(\mathsf{d}(p,x)<\frac{\mathsf{d}(s,p)}{\beta}.\) Using \(p\in A_i(s)\) and triangle inequality, \(\mathsf{d}(s,x)<\left(1+\frac{1}{\beta}\right)\left(r_{i+1}+\frac{r_i}{\alpha+2}\right),\) and \(\mathsf{d}(s,x)>\left(1-\frac{1}{\beta}\right)\left(r_i-\frac{r_i}{\alpha+2}\right)=r_i\cdot\frac{\alpha+1}{\alpha+2}\left(1-\frac{1}{\beta}\right).\) Thus, for a fixed edge (_s,x_), the relevant values of _ri_ lie in an interval whose ratio is at most \(R_\beta=\frac{\left((1+\delta)+\frac{1}{\alpha+2}\right)\left(1+\frac{1}{\beta}\right)}{\frac{\alpha+1}{\alpha+2}\left(1-\frac{1}{\beta}\right)}\)
\(=\frac{\alpha^2+4\alpha+2}{\alpha(\alpha+1)}\cdot\frac{2\alpha+9+\frac{4}{\alpha}}{2\alpha+7+\frac{4}{\alpha}}\)
\(\le\left(1+\frac{1}{\alpha}\right)^3\cdot\left(1+\frac{1}{\alpha}\right)\le\left(1+\frac{1}{\alpha}\right)^4.\) Since consecutive values of _ri_ differ by a factor of \(1+1/\alpha\), there are at most \(1+\mathrm{log}_{1+1/\alpha} R_\beta\le 5\) such levels.

By Claim 2.4, for each fixed level _i_, at most one pair (_i,p_) is mapped to any given edge of \(E_s^\star\). By Claim 2.5, such pairs occur at no more than 5 levels for each edge. Therefore,

\(|E_s|\le\sum_{i=0}^L|E_s^i|\le 5|E_s^\star|.\)

Summing over all sources \(s\in P\) gives \(|E|\le 5|E^\star|\).

## 2.5 Logarithmic Bicriteria Approximation.

**Lemma 2.6.** _Let_ (_P,_d) _be a metric space of n points and let_ \(\alpha\ge 1\)_. Let G_=(_P,E_) _be the graph returned by Algorithm 2.4. Then G is an_ \((\alpha,\beta')\)_-bicriteria_ 8(ln_n_+1)_-approximation, where_

\(\beta'=(1+\delta)(\alpha+2)+2=\alpha+5+\frac{2}{\alpha}.\)

_Proof._ Let _G<sup>⋆</sup>_=(_P,E<sup>⋆</sup>_) be a sparsest \(\beta'\)-navigable graph. Fix a source point \(s\in P\) and a level _i_. Write \(E_s^\star=\{(s,x)\in E^\star\}\) for the outgoing edges of _s_ in _G<sup>⋆</sup>_. Write \(\rho_i=r_i/(\alpha+2)\), and let \(\mathcal{G}_i=\{(C_j,p_j)\}_j\) be the greedy ball cover at level _i_ in the order in which the clusters are produced.

Define

\(\mathcal{U}_{i,s}=\bigcup\{C_j|(C_j,p_j)\in\mathcal{G}_i,p_j\in A_i(s)\}.\)

Let \(\mathcal{F}_{i,s}=\{B(c,\rho_i)\cap\mathcal{U}_{i,s}|c\in P\}\), and let OPT<sub>_i,s_</sub> be the optimum set-cover value for the instance (U<sub>_i,s_</sub>,F<sub>_i,s_</sub>).

**Claim 2.7.** _For every source s and level i,_<tbc>

\(|E_s^i|\le(lnn+1)\text{OPT}_{i,s}.\)

<tbc>_Proof of claim._ Write the output of Algorithm 2.2 at level _i_ as<tbc>

\((C_1,p_1),(C_2,p_2),\dots,(C_m,p_m),\)

<tbc>in the order in which the clusters are produced. Let _U_<sup>(_j_)</sup> be the set of points that remain uncovered immediately before the _j_-th greedy step. Thus<tbc>

\(C_j=U^{(j)}\cap B(p_j,\rho_i),\)

<tbc>and the greedy choice of _p<sub>j</sub>_ implies that, for every center \(c\in P\),

\(|C_j|=|U^{(j)}\cap B(p_j,\rho_i)|\ge|U^{(j)}\cap B(c,\rho_i)|.\) (2.1)

Define \(J_{i,s}=\{j\in[m]|p_j\in A_i(s)\}\). Then \(E_s^i\) contains exactly one edge (_s,p<sub>j</sub>_) for each \(j\in J_{i,s}\), and<tbc>

\(\mathcal{U}_{i,s}=\bigcup_{j\in J_{i,s}}C_j.\)

<tbc>For every point \(v\in C_j\), define its weight by<tbc>

\(y_v=\frac{1}{|C_j|}.\)

Thus each greedy step assigns total weight 1 to the points newly covered at that step. For each \(j\in J_{i,s}\), the total weight of the points in _Cj_ is \(\sum_{v\in C_j}y_v=1.\) Therefore \(\sum_{v\in\mathcal{U}_{i,s}}y_v=\sum_{j\in J_{i,s}}\sum_{v\in C_j}y_v=|J_{i,s}|=|E_s^i|.\) (2.2) For this fixed level _i_, the weights _yv_ are determined by the greedy Set Cover execution on all of _P_ and do not depend on the source _s_. We use these same weights to bound \(|E_s^i|\) for every local instance (U_i,s,_F_i,s_). We next bound the total weight in any radius-\(\rho_i\) ball: for every \(c\in P\), \(\sum_{v\in B(c,\rho_i)}y_v\le H_n\le lnn+1,\) (2.3) where \(H_n=1+1/2+\cdots+1/n\). Fix such a ball \(Q=B(c,\rho_i)\). Consider only the greedy steps that cover at least one point of _Q_. Immediately before such a step _j_, let \(k_j=|Q\cap U^{(j)}|\) be the number of still-uncovered points of _Q_, and let \(q_j=|Q\cap C_j|\) be the number of points of _Q_ covered at this step. Since _Q_ itself is one of the available radius-\(\rho_i\) balls, the candidate center _c_ would cover all _kj_ currently uncovered points of _Q_. Hence, by (2.1), \(|C_j|\ge k_j.\) The total weight of the _qj_ points of _Q_ covered at step _j_ is \(\frac{q_j}{|C_j|}\le\frac{q_j}{k_j}.\) If the nonzero values of _kj_ along these steps are denoted by \(k^{(1)}>k^{(2)}>\cdots>k^{(a)}>0,\) and _q_(_h_)=_k_(_h_)-_k_(_h_+1) with _k_(_a_+1)=0, then \(\sum_{v\in B(c,\rho_i)}y_v\le\sum_{h=1}^a\frac{q^{(h)}}{k^{(h)}}\le\sum_{h=1}^a\sum_{\ell=k^{(h+1)}+1}^{k^{(h)}}\frac{1}{\ell}=H_{k^{(1)}}\le H_n.\) This proves (2.3). Now let Bopt be an optimal cover of U_i,s_ by sets from F_i,s_, so |Bopt|=OPT_i,s_. Each set in Bopt has the form \(B(c,\rho_i)\cap\mathcal{U}_{i,s}\) for some \(c\in P\). Since \(y_v\ge 0\) for every \(v\in P\) and Bopt covers U_i,s_, \(|E_s^i|=\sum_{v\in\mathcal{U}_{i,s}}y_v\text{by (2.2)}\)
\(\le\sum_{B(c,\rho_i)\cap\mathcal{U}_{i,s}\in\mathcal{B}^\mathrm{opt}}\sum_{v\in B(c,\rho_i)\cap\mathcal{U}_{i,s}}y_v\)
\(\le\sum_{B(c,\rho_i)\cap\mathcal{U}_{i,s}\in\mathcal{B}^\mathrm{opt}}\sum_{v\in B(c,\rho_i)}y_v\)
\(\le H_n\cdot|\mathcal{B}^\mathrm{opt}|\le(lnn+1)\mathrm{OPT}_{i,s},\) where the penultimate inequality uses (2.3). This proves the claim.

**Claim 2.8.** _If an edge_ \((s,x)\in E^\star\) _is a_ \(\beta'\)_-navigation from s to a point_ \(v\in\mathcal{U}_{i,s}\)_, then_ \(v\in B(x,\rho_i)\). _Proof of claim._ Since \(v\in\mathcal{U}_{i,s}\), there exists a pair \((C,p)\in\mathcal{G}_i\) such that \(v\in C\) and \(p\in A_i(s)\). Hence \(\mathsf{d}(p,v)\le\rho_i\). By triangle inequality, \(\mathsf{d}(s,v)\le\mathsf{d}(s,p)+\mathsf{d}(p,v)\le r_{i+1}+2\rho_i=r_i\left(1+\delta+\frac{2}{\alpha+2}\right).\) If (_s,x_) is a \(\beta'\)-navigation from _s_ to _v_, then \(\mathsf{d}(x,v)<\frac{\mathsf{d}(s,v)}{\beta'}\le\frac{r_i\left(1+\delta+\frac{2}{\alpha+2}\right)}{(1+\delta)(\alpha+2)+2}=\frac{r_i}{\alpha+2}=\rho_i.\) Thus \(v\in B(x,\rho_i)\). For each level _i_, define \(E_{s,i}^\star=\left\{(s,x)\in E_s^\star\middle|\exists v\in\mathcal{U}_{i,s}\text{such that}\mathsf{d}(x,v)<\frac{\mathsf{d}(s,v)}{\beta'}\right\}.\) By the \(\beta'\)-navigability of _G⋆_ and Claim 2.8, the balls \(\{B(x,\rho_i)\cap\mathcal{U}_{i,s}|(s,x)\in E_{s,i}^\star\}\) cover U_i,s_. Therefore, \(\mathsf{OPT}_{i,s}\le|E_{s,i}^\star|.\) It remains to show that each edge of \(E_s^\star\) belongs to only constantly many sets \(E_{s,i}^\star\). Suppose \((s,x)\in E_{s,i}^\star\). Then there exists \(v\in\mathcal{U}_{i,s}\) such that \(\mathsf{d}(x,v)<\mathsf{d}(s,v)/\beta'\). Choose a pair \((C,p)\in\mathcal{G}_i\) with \(v\in C\) and \(p\in A_i(s)\). Since \(\mathsf{d}(p,v)\le\rho_i\), \(\mathsf{d}(s,v)\le r_{i+1}+2\rho_i=r_i\left(1+\delta+\frac{2}{\alpha+2}\right),\) and \(\mathsf{d}(s,v)>r_i-2\rho_i=r_i\left(1-\frac{2}{\alpha+2}\right).\) Consequently, \(r_i\left(1-\frac{2}{\alpha+2}\right)\left(1-\frac{1}{\beta'}\right)<\mathsf{d}(s,x)Thus, for a fixed edge (_s,x_), the relevant values of _ri_ lie in an interval whose ratio is at most \(R_{\beta^\prime}=\frac{\left(1+\delta+\frac{2}{\alpha+2}\right)\left(1+\frac{1}{\beta'}\right)}{\left(1-\frac{2}{\alpha+2}\right)\left(1-\frac{1}{\beta'}\right)}\)
\(=\frac{\alpha^2+5\alpha+2}{\alpha^2}\cdot\frac{\alpha+6+\frac{2}{\alpha}}{\alpha+4+\frac{2}{\alpha}}\)
\(\le\left(1+\frac{1}{\alpha}\right)^5\cdot\left(1+\frac{1}{\alpha}\right)^2=\left(1+\frac{1}{\alpha}\right)^7.\)

<tbc>Since consecutive values of _r<sub>i</sub>_ differ by a factor of \(1+1/\alpha\), the edge (_s,x_) can belong to at most \(1+log_{1+1/\alpha} R_{\beta^\prime}\le 8\) sets \(E_{s,i}^\star\). Hence<tbc>

\(\sum_{i=0}^LOPT_{i,s}\le\sum_{i=0}^L|E_{s,i}^\star|\le 8|E_s^\star|.\)

<tbc>Combining this with Claim 2.7,

\(|E_s|\le\sum_{i=0}^L|E_s^i|\le(lnn+1)\sum_{i=0}^LOPT_{i,s}\le 8(lnn+1)|E_s^\star|.\)

Summing over all sources \(s\in P\) gives \(|E|\le 8(lnn+1)|E^\star|\).

### 2.6 Combining the Two Constructions.

_Proof of Theorem 1.4._ Run both Algorithm 2.3 and Algorithm 2.4, and return the graph with fewer edges. By Lemma 2.2, both candidate graphs are \(\alpha\)-navigable, so the returned graph is also \(\alpha\)- navigable. If _G_<sub>const</sub> is the graph returned by Algorithm 2.3 and _G_<sub>log</sub> is the graph returned by Algorithm 2.4, then the final output _G_ satisfies

\(|E(G)|\le|E(G_\mathrm{const})|\text{and}|E(G)|\le|E(G_\mathrm{log})|.\)

Therefore Lemma 2.3 gives the \((\alpha,2\alpha+8+4/\alpha)\)-bicriteria 5-approximation guarantee, and Lemma 2.6 gives the \((\alpha,\alpha+5+2/\alpha)\)-bicriteria _O_(ln_n_)-approximation guarantee. The running time remains \(\tilde{O}(\alpha n^2log\Delta)\), which is \(\tilde{O}(n^2log\Delta)\) for constant \(\alpha\).

## 3 Hardness Proof.

In this section we prove Theorem 1.5. We reduce Set Cover to \((\alpha,2\alpha-\eta)\)-bicriteria approximation of \(\alpha\)-navigable graphs on metric point sets.

**Lemma 3.1** (\[DS13\])**.** _Let_ (U,F) _be a set cover instance with n elements and m=n<sup>d</sup> sets for some constant d=O_(1)_. It is NP-hard to compute a_ \(\frac{1}{2}lnn\)_-approximation of minimum set cover._

_Proof of Theorem 1.5._ Fix constants \(\alpha\ge 1\) and \(\eta\in(0,1)\). Let (U,F) be a hard Set Cover instance from Lemma 3.1, with _n_ elements and \(m\le n^d\) sets for a constant _d=O_(1). We may assume that the instance is feasible and that its optimum value |_C<sup>⋆</sup>_| is at least 20: if |_C<sup>⋆</sup>|\<_20, then the optimum can be found by exhaustive search over all subsets of at most 19 sets, which takes polynomial time because _d_ is a constant.

### Reduction from Set Cover to \((\alpha,2\alpha-\eta)\)-Bicriteria Approximation.

Let<tbc>

\(K=\left\lceil\frac{2(m+n+1)}{\eta}\right\rceil.\)

<tbc>We create _K_ disjoint copies of the Set Cover instance, denoted by (U_<sub>i</sub>,_F_<sub>i</sub>_) for \(1\le i\le K\). We represent each set and each element by a distinct vertex, using the same notation for the vertex and the object it represents. For each copy _i_, we also introduce a unique hub point _c<sub>i</sub>_, and write<tbc>

\(P_i=\{c_i\}\cup\mathcal{F}_i\cup\mathcal{U}_i,P=\bigcup_{i=1}^KP_i.\)

Thus the number of metric points is _N_=|_P_|=_K(m+n_+1).

To define the metric (_P,_d), we construct an undirected weighted graph \(H=(P,F,\mu)\) and let \(\mathsf{d}(\cdot,\cdot)\) be the shortest-path metric of _H_. The edges and weights in _H_ are defined as follows; see Figure 1 for an illustration.

1. For each \(i\in[K]\), if element \(e\in\mathcal{U}_i\) is contained in set \(S\in\mathcal{F}_i\), add an edge (_S,e_) with weight \(\mu(S,e)=1\).<tbc>

2. For each \(i\in[K]\), add an edge (_c<sub>i</sub>,S_) with weight \(\mu(c_i,S)=1\) for every \(S\in\mathcal{F}_i\).<tbc>

3. For any two points \(p\in P_i\) and \(q\in P_j\) with \(i\neq j\), add an edge (_p,q_) with weight \(\mu(p,q)=2\alpha\).

Now run a polynomial-time \((\alpha,2\alpha-\eta)\)-bicriteria approximation algorithm on this metric and let _G_=(_P,E_) be the resulting \(\alpha\)-navigable graph. Among all pairs (_s,j_) with \(s\in P_i\) and \(i,j\in[K]\), \(i\neq j\), choose one that minimizes the number of out-neighbors of _s_ in \(\mathcal{F}_j\cup\mathcal{U}_j\). Denote by \(V_{s,j}=\{p\in\mathcal{F}_j\cup\mathcal{U}_j:(s,p)\in E\}\) the set of these out-neighbors.

**Lemma 3.2.** _The set_ \(V_{s,j}\cap\mathcal{F}_j\) _forms a set cover of_ U_<sub>j</sub>_\\_V<sub>s,j</sub>._

_Proof._ Consider any element \(x\in\mathcal{U}_j\backslash V_{s,j}\). Since _G_ is \(\alpha\)-navigable, there exists an edge \((s,p)\in E\) such that \(\mathsf{d}(p,x)<\mathsf{d}(s,x)/\alpha\). Since _s_ and _x_ belong to different copies, \(\mathsf{d}(s,x)=2\alpha\), and hence d(_p,x)\<_2. All edge weights in _H_ are at least 1, and the only points at distance strictly less than 2 from _x_ are the sets in F_<sub>j</sub>_ that contain _x_. Moreover, \(x\notin V_{s,j}\), so \(p\neq x\). Therefore \(p\in V_{s,j}\cap\mathcal{F}_j\) and _p_ contains _x_.

For every element \(v\in\mathcal{U}_j\cap V_{s,j}\), choose an arbitrary set \(S_v\in\mathcal{F}_j\) containing _v_, which exists because the original Set Cover instance is feasible. Define

\(C=(V_{s,j}\cap\mathcal{F}_j)\cup\{S_v:v\in\mathcal{U}_j\cap V_{s,j}\}.\)

By Lemma 3.2, _C_ is a valid set cover for the _j_-th copy, and therefore for the original instance, with \(|C|\le|V_{s,j}|\).

## Approximation Analysis. Let _C⋆_ be an optimal set cover solution for the original instance. For each index _i_, let \(C_i^\star\) be a copy of _C⋆_ but on the set system (U_i,_F_i_). We construct a \((2\alpha-\eta)\)-navigable graph _G⋆_=(_P,E⋆_) as follows. • **Inter-copy edges:** For every pair of distinct indices \(i,j\in[K]\) and every \(s\in P_i\), add edges from _s_ to _cj_ and to every point in \(C_j^\star\). • **Intra-copy edges:** For every \(i\in[K]\) and every pair of distinct points \(s,t\in P_i\), add the directed edge (_s,t_). We first verify that _G⋆_ is \((2\alpha-\eta)\)-navigable. If _s_ and _t_ belong to the same copy, then the direct edge (_s,t_) gives distance 0 to the target. Otherwise, suppose \(s\in P_i\) and \(t\in P_j\) for \(j\neq i\). Then \(\mathsf{d}(s,t)=2\alpha\). If _t=cj_ or \(t\in C_j^\star\), the direct edge to _t_ again gives distance 0. If \(t\in\mathcal{F}_j\backslash C_j^\star\), then the edge (_s,cj_) satisfies \(\mathsf{d}(c_j,t)=1<\frac{2\alpha}{2\alpha-\eta}=\frac{\mathsf{d}(s,t)}{2\alpha-\eta}.\) Finally, if \(t\in\mathcal{U}_j\), then some set \(S\in C_j^\star\) contains _t_, and the edge (_s,S_) satisfies \(\mathsf{d}(S,t)=1<\frac{2\alpha}{2\alpha-\eta}=\frac{\mathsf{d}(s,t)}{2\alpha-\eta}.\) Thus _G⋆_ is \((2\alpha-\eta)\)-navigable. The total number of edges in _G⋆_ is \(|E^\star|=K(K-1)(m+n+1)(|C^\star|+1)+K(m+n+1)(m+n).\) Suppose _G_=(_P,E_) is an \((\alpha,2\alpha-\eta)\)-bicriteria \(\rho\)-approximation to the sparsest \(\alpha\)-navigable graph, where \(\rho=\frac{1}{10d}lnN\). Since _G⋆_ is feasible for the comparison parameter \(2\alpha-\eta\), we have \(|E|\le\rho|E^\star|\). Averaging over the _K(K_-1)(_m+n_+1) pairs (_s,j_) with \(s\in P_i\) and \(i,j\in[K]\), \(i\neq j\), shows that the chosen pair (_s,j_) satisfies \(|C|\le|V_{s,j}|\le\frac{|E|}{K(K-1)(m+n+1)}\)
\(\le\rho\left(|C^\star|+1+\frac{m+n}{K-1}\right)\)
\(\le\rho\left(|C^\star|+1+\eta\right).\) Here the last inequality follows from the choice of _K_. Since \(m\le n^d\) and \(\eta\) is a fixed constant, for all sufficiently large _n_ we have \(N=K(m+n+1)\le\frac{100n^{2d}}{\eta}.\) Therefore \(\rho=\frac{1}{10d}lnN\le\frac{1}{10d}ln\left(\frac{100n^{2d}}{\eta}\right)<0.21lnn\) for all sufficiently large _n_. Also, by our assumption \(|C^\star|\ge 20\) and by \(\eta<1\), \(|C^\star|+1+\eta\le|C^\star|+2\le 1.1|C^\star|.\)

<tbc>Combining the above inequalities, we get

\(|C|<0.21lnn\cdot 1.1|C^\star|<\frac{1}{2}lnn\cdot|C^\star|,\)

contradicting Lemma 3.1. Thus, for \(c_\eta=1/(10d)\), no polynomial-time \((\alpha,2\alpha-\eta)\)-bicriteria \(c_\eta lnN\)- approximation exists unless P=NP. \(\square\)
